analysis.one_liner: Expands patent law so that patented-process information itself counts as an infringing product.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change patent law to define a 'product' as including not just physical goods but also information in any fixed format. That would let patent holders argue that information — such as data or software produced using a patented process — can infringe a patent, extending patent enforcement beyond physical products. It applied retroactively to patents granted before or after enactment, while protecting already-final court decisions.
analysis.who_benefits: Patent holders — companies, universities, and others holding process patents — gain a new way to enforce those patents against information itself, not just the physical goods made with the patented process. That broadens the scope and value of their existing patents.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a definition to patent law making 'product' include both physical goods and information in any fixed format, so information generated by a patented process can be treated as an infringing product.
The change applies to any patent granted before, on, or after enactment, expanding the reach of existing patents.
The bill states its purpose is to promote research among universities, the public sector, and private enterprise in the informatics realm.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who creates, stores, or uses information produced with a patented process could face new infringement claims — software developers, researchers, data-driven businesses, and ultimately the people who pay higher prices for information products and services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Users and producers of information products

drawbacks.text: Treating information itself as a patentable-infringement 'product' would create legal uncertainty for software developers, researchers, and data businesses, who could face infringement claims over information they never physically copied.
Applying the change to patents granted before enactment subjects existing information practices to new liability, raising costs that businesses would pass to customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered patent holders a broad new enforcement tool framed as promoting research, but its main effect would have been to expand patent liability into the information economy. The potential benefit to research collaboration is speculative; the added litigation risk for anyone working with data or software would have been concrete.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then sent to a subcommittee in February 2006, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Gerlach introduced the bill on November 2, 2005, with no cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
On February 6, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where it stayed for the rest of the 109th Congress.
No hearing, markup, floor action, or vote ever took place, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died quietly, patent holders did not gain the expanded information-infringement right, and businesses and researchers who work with information avoided the new liability it would have created. There was little apparent support behind the bill, so little was lost by its failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Information businesses and researchers, for now

for.name: Rep. Jim Gerlach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security
against.role: Subcommittee with jurisdiction after February 2006 referral
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there is no record of party positions on either side.

industries.industry: Patent holders (pharmaceutical, chemical, and technology companies holding process patents)
industries.note: The bill would have let these patent holders claim that information in fixed format — not just physical goods — infringes their patents, expanding enforcement and the value of existing patents. The cost would show up as higher prices and litigation risk across the information economy.

industries.industry: Software developers, researchers, and data-driven businesses
industries.note: Anyone creating, storing, or using information generated by a patented process could face new infringement claims, raising legal costs and discouraging research and data work. Ordinary people would feel this through higher prices and less innovation.
